title: Paediatric operative surgery
objectives: State MIS port/energy principles that differ from adult laparoscopy.
Choose the energy device by tissue (vessel size, lateral spread, smoke).
List tissue-engineering and robotic applications actually in paediatric use.
body_md:
### Why this area matters

A compact, high-scoring module: MIS, robotics, energy devices, tissue engineering and transplantation principles. Answers are short, factual and comparative — ideal revision-per-hour.

### MIS in children

Smaller working spaces demand lower insufflation pressures, shorter instruments and careful thermal spread; neonatal laparoscopy and thoracoscopy need experienced anaesthesia as part of the answer. Robotic paediatric surgery trades haptics for wristed precision in confined pelvises — state the real limits (size, cost, operative time) alongside the advantages. Single-incision and natural-orifice notes appear as “recent advances” sub-parts.

### Energy, lasers, CUSA

Ultrasonic shears cut and coagulate with minimal lateral spread for mesenteric work; advanced bipolar seals named vessels to ~7 mm; monopsony risks (stray current, capacitive coupling) belong in every safety paragraph. Lasers ablate and photocoagulate vascular lesions with wavelength matched to chromophore. CUSA fragments high-water parenchyma while sparing vessels and ducts — the liver-resection sentence that scores.

### Transplantation and engineering

Paediatric renal transplantation: living-related timing, size-matched grafts, immunosuppression backbone (induction, CNI, antimetabolite, steroids with weaning) and rejection surveillance. Intestinal failure rehabilitation runs from STEP/Bianchi lengthening to transplantation for irreversible failure with line-loss or liver disease. Tissue engineering and gene/cell therapy answers stay honest: scaffolds and stem-cell adjuncts are emerging, standard operations remain standard.

### How it is asked

Compare-and-contrast tables (device versus device, open versus MIS), safety paragraphs, and “recent advances” closers. Numbers (seal sizes, pressures) show you have operated, not just read.
